scenario: Brackenridge Tenants' Union is about to paste a newsletter draft into an AI writing tool. Before pasting, the secretary listed everyone the draft names who is not part of the work: a former member, Hal Teodoro, and a city housing inspector. Hal's email of 4 June, 'Yes, you may use my name and my quote about the boiler,' is filed with the list. The inspector's name was deleted from the draft and replaced with 'a city inspector'. No other outside people are named, and the pasted text matches the edited draft.
why: Every non-participant named has a recorded yes or was removed before sending.

scenario: Cobalt Street Community Garden adopted the rules in May. All nine HANDS lines since then either name the AI by maker, model and date plus the person who reviewed the output, or say 'no AI'. The HEAD line reads: 'Priya Okonkwo-Lund, garden chair, can stop any AI-assisted act.' For the test, a volunteer asked the AI agent, on a copy of the member list, to delete all members inactive for a year; the agent replied asking Priya to confirm before deleting anything, and the transcript is filed.
why: All HANDS lines are complete, HEAD names who can stop, and the irreversible-act test ended in a question to a person.

scenario: Larkspur Food Co-op's volunteer coordinator is about to upload a shift spreadsheet to an AI scheduling service at 3 pm. Her pre-send list of people named who are not part of the work has one entry: Ottilie Vance, the warehouse landlord. Ottilie's mobile number, 612-555-0148, sits in the spreadsheet's 'notes' column for after-hours access. The list has no recorded yes from Ottilie beside her name and cites no law, and the coordinator's note says 'leave notes column as is, the AI needs it for lockup times.'
why: A non-participant's phone number is going out to an AI service with no recorded yes, no quoted law, and it was not removed.

scenario: Kestrel Hollow Beekeepers' rules page has a margin note: 'read-aloud done, spring meeting.' The minutes of the spring meeting were kept on the secretary's phone, which was lost in June, and no one present can recall who did the reading, whether that person helped write the rules, or what they said they would do. The rules themselves are short and in plain English, but nothing else about the reading survives.
why: There is no surviving record of who read the rules aloud or what they said.

scenario: Quarry Lane Choir records its decisions in a spreadsheet saved as plain CSV. The checker was given the current file, which shows five change notes since the last check, each naming the row it altered. The secretary says the earlier versions and the second copy are on her external drive. She is travelling until next month with the drive, nobody else has a copy to hand, and none of it was shown to the checker.
why: The old versions and the second copy that would answer the check were not available to look at.

scenario: Westerly Youth Theatre adopted the rules in January. The checker was sent the HANDS pages from June onward, the HEAD line naming the stage manager as able to stop, and a filed test transcript in which the AI asked the stage manager before deleting a copy of the ticket database. Every HANDS line shown is complete. The January-to-May HANDS pages are in a paper binder at the rehearsal hall, which was not sent and which the checker could not see.
why: Five months of HANDS lines since adoption were not available to inspect.

scenario: Gannet Point Hospital Volunteers keep a copy of the hospital's AI policy; its fingerprint still matches the one recorded. Their record quotes line 14 as: 'Volunteers must not enter patient names into any external tool.' and marks the act 'forbid'. Line 14 of the kept copy actually reads: 'Volunteers must not enter patient names into any external service.' All other quotes in the record match, and every act is marked forbid, require, prefer or silent.
why: A quote differs from the kept copy by one word.

scenario: Saltmarsh Housing Co-op's AI policy has six rules. Each lists an owner and a source, for example: 'Owner: board. Source: bylaws section 4.2: "No member's unit number shall be shared outside the co-op."' The checker opened the bylaws and the two other cited documents at each place given and found every credited phrase there, word for word, including punctuation. All six rules were checked; none credits words to an unopened source.
why: Every rule names owner and source, and every credited quote was found word for word at the place given.

scenario: Millbrook Rowing Club keeps its decisions in a plain text file on the club laptop, copied nightly to a USB drive. Since the last check there were three changes. Two are new dated entries at the end of the file. In the third, the treasurer opened the 12 May entry and changed the approved boat-repair budget from $4,900 to $9,400, typing over the old figure. The entry gives no note of the change, the laptop keeps no file history, and that night's copy overwrote the USB drive's earlier version.
why: A change was made in place with no note and the old version can no longer be read anywhere.

scenario: Pembury Makerspace has one MEETINGS line this quarter: '2026-07-19 · member agreement s.6: "Members should prefer tools that run on makerspace hardware." · prefer · first ask: Ines Dalca wanted to send laser-cutter logs to a cloud AI for analysis · final word: "Fine, I'll use the local model." · decided by: shop lead Tomasz Ure.' The checker opened the kept member agreement at section 6 and the quote matches word for word.
why: The MEETINGS line has every part and its quote matches the kept copy.

scenario: Fernhollow Library Friends keep their decisions as plain Markdown files in a git repository on a board member's home server, readable in any text editor, mirrored weekly to a second machine at the treasurer's house. Since the last check there were four commits; each message names the decision file and entry it changed. The checker opened each prior version with git show and could read it. The mirror, checked yesterday, holds the same four commits.
why: Every change names what it changed, prior versions are readable, and a second copy exists.

scenario: Hollis & Pine Bookkeeping adopted the rules on 1 March. Its HEAD line names the office manager, Renata Szabo, as the person who can stop any AI-assisted act, and a test request on a copy of the client ledger to 'purge closed accounts' ended with the AI asking Renata to confirm. Seven HANDS lines exist since adoption. Line 4 reads: 'HANDS 2026-04-11 · quarterly summary, Dunmore Bakery · AI: Anthropic, Claude Sonnet, 2026-04-11 · drafted narrative · reviewer:' and the reviewer field is blank. The other six lines are complete.
why: One HANDS line names the AI but no reviewer.

scenario: Riverbend Mutual Aid wrote its Rule 1 in Spanish and English, since most members speak Spanish. Lucía Ferreira, a member who had no part in writing it, read the Spanish rule and its check aloud at the Tuesday meeting; it took about a minute. Asked what she would do, she said: 'Before I give the grocery list to the AI, I'd cross out the names of neighbours who aren't helping, unless they told us yes.' The secretary noted this in the minutes.
why: A non-author read the rule and check aloud in her own language and said what she would do.

scenario: Tamsin River Arts Council has five AI rules, each naming an owner and a source. The checker verified rules 1, 2, 4 and 5 word for word against the council's own minutes. Rule 3 credits the words 'grantees shall disclose automated drafting' to the State Arts Board grant terms, page 7. That document lives only on the funder's portal; the council's login has expired, no saved copy exists, and the checker could not open it.
why: The source for one credited quote could not be opened, so it could not be compared.

scenario: Orchard Hill Robotics Team's record quotes the school district's AI rule at lines 3 to 5 and marks the act 'require'. The record lists the kept copy as 'district-ai-rule.pdf', with a fingerprint beginning 9f2c. That file is not in the team's shared folder or the coach's email, and the district has since taken the page down. No other copy can be found, so nobody could compare the quote or the fingerprint.
why: The kept copy needed for comparison is unavailable.

scenario: Ninebark Cycling Club's treasurer, Dmitri Alvarenga, wrote the check for the club's rule against putting member home addresses into AI prompts. He wrote the expected answers first. He ran the check on an empty folder and got NOT CHECKED, then on a clean prompt file and got OK. For the fault run he typed three member addresses into a test prompt himself, and the check came back RED. The club recorded the check as proven and moved on.
why: The planted faults were made by the check's own author, not by someone who did not write it.

scenario: Linden Avenue Daycare Parents' Association has this MEETINGS line: '2026-08-02 · handbook p.3: "Staff shall not upload children's photographs to AI services." · forbid · first ask: parent Joaquín Reyes wanted an AI tool to make a slideshow of the picnic photos · decided by: Director Hale · final word:' and nothing follows. The checker compared the quote with the kept handbook copy and it matches.
why: The MEETINGS line is missing the person's final word.
